turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this screen's frozen again. Give me a second. Right, Mrs Khumalo, what's been going on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Doctor, I'm Lerato, I stay with her in the flat. Her ankles have been swelling, and the pill box is a proper mess.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja the swelling, but she's making it sound worse. It's mostly this right one, not both.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? Something just beeped. Swelling where?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): My right ankle. It gets puffy by the afternoon. Is it my heart, doctor? I keep thinking that.
[SEG0006] person_2 (CAREGIVER): It's been three weeks, both ankles, you can see the sock marks at night.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Ag no, not three weeks. More like ten days, since we got back from my sister in Polokwane. And the left one is fine.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, so somewhere between ten days and three weeks. The file's still loading. Any pain in the ankle, or just the puffiness?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): No pain. It just looks fat. Is fat a silly word? Sorry, I'm nervous.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not silly. Short of breath at all? Chest pain?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No chest pain. I'm not short of breath. I just get tired on the stairs.
[SEG0012] person_2 (CAREGIVER): She is dizzy in the mornings, doctor. She holds the wall by the kitchen.
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm not dizzy. I just feel wobbly if I stand up too quick. That's different, ne?
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wobbly, not spinning. Sorry, can you repeat how often? I was typing in the wrong box.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Most mornings. Not every single day. Maybe four times this week. Is it a stroke? Should I be worried?
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't think it's a stroke from what you're saying. I'm not adding anything until I've seen the tablets. Who packs them?
[SEG0017] person_2 (CAREGIVER): I do. There's the water tablet, the little white one, a pink one, and the sugar one. The cholesterol one the other doctor stopped.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which doctor, and what was that cholesterol tablet called? Say it slowly, hey.
[SEG0019] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Doctor Pillay at the hospital clinic, about two months back. Simvastatin. He stopped it because her legs were cramping.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja those cramps were horrible at night. They're better now. If you change my tablets will they come back?
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll get there. The water tablet, what dose is she on now?
[SEG0022] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Furosemide, forty milligrams... ag, no, sorry, twenty milligrams. It was dropped from forty to twenty. Once in the morning.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): I take it with my rooibos, before breakfast. Is twenty even enough? My neighbour takes more than that.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Neighbours aren't a script, hey. You mentioned a little white one and a pink one for the pressure?
[SEG0025] person_2 (CAREGIVER): The little white one is perindopril, four milligrams, mornings. The pink one is Coversyl, also for the high blood. I wrote them as two things on my paper.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on, I'm opening the medication list. Coversyl is perindopril. Same medicine, different jacket. So it's been double-counted.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Eish. So I've been swallowing two? I knew it. Is that why the ankle went fat?
[SEG0028] person_2 (CAREGIVER): No, Mama. I only pack the white one. The pink bottle is an old one from Clicks. I just wrote it down twice by mistake.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): You sure? I saw a pink one at supper on Tuesday. I don't imagine things.
[SEG0030] person_2 (CAREGIVER): That was my vitamin, shame, not yours. Yours is only the little white one.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, repeat that? Whose vitamin? This cursor keeps jumping.
[SEG0032] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Mine. Hers is perindopril four milligrams once every morning. The little white tablet, not the pink.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, then we won't count it twice. On your file I've got high blood and sugar. There's something for the sugar as well?
[SEG0034] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Metformin, five hundred milligrams, twice a day with meals. She's been on it five years... no, since twenty nineteen, so six years.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): And I don't skip it. The sugar going high scares me. What was my last one, doctor? The chemist machine said something ugly.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Last month's lab is here. The HbA1c was seven point two percent. Not ugly. Blood pressure, the sister wrote one fifty two over ninety four... no, that's the old visit. Today is one thirty eight over eighty four, pulse seventy six.
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Is one thirty eight safe? What if I fall? The passage is dark when load shedding hits, and I'm seventy eight, you know.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): One thirty eight over eighty four is acceptable. I'm not adding a new pressure tablet. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I can take anything. Is that still normal at my age?
[SEG0040] person_2 (CAREGIVER): No drug allergies, doctor. She does get heartburn if she takes the metformin without food, but that's not an allergy.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ja, that's just irritation, not an allergy. Let me press the ankles. Right one has pitting oedema. Left side is basically flat.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): See, I told her it's the right. Is the water tablet failing? Should I sleep with my legs up? I already use a cushion.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): The cushion is fine, keep doing that. I think the furosemide at twenty is a bit light for this swelling. I'm going to increase it to forty milligrams each morning.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Forty? But it was just brought down. Won't I live in the loo? Some days the clinic transport comes at seven.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): You'll pass more water for a few days, mostly morning if you take it when you wake, not at night. If you get cramps or you feel faint, phone us.
[SEG0046] person_2 (CAREGIVER): Must I throw the twenty milligram tablets away, or can she use two of them to make forty?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two of the twenties is fine until the new script is ready. I'll send forty milligram tablets to the chemist, one each morning. The medical aid should cover it.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): And the little white one stays? Do I need the cholesterol tablet back? My sister had a stroke and now I can't stop thinking about it.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Perindopril stays, four milligrams once a day, only the white tablet. I'm not restarting the simvastatin today. Cholesterol can wait, it's not the ankle.
[SEG0050] person_2 (CAREGIVER): When must we come back? Should I bring that old pink bottle so you can see it?

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): You can bring the bottles if you like, but you don't have to. Come back in two weeks so I can check the swelling and the pressure. If the swelling is worse before that, or she gets breathless, don't wait, come in.
